content: An oral ulcer, also known as a mouth ulcer, is an open sore that develops inside the mouth due to a disruption in the mucous membrane or the epithelial lining. These ulcers can occur on the lips, inside the cheeks, or around the mouth. They are caused by a variety of factors, including physical or chemical trauma, infections from microorganisms or viruses, underlying medical conditions, medications, cancerous processes, or nonspecific mechanisms. Once an ulcer forms, it may persist due to ongoing inflammation or secondary infection. Two common types of oral ulcers are aphthous ulcers (commonly referred to as canker sores) and cold sores, the latter being caused by the herpes simplex virus. Causes of Oral Ulcers Common Causes Oral ulcers can result from numerous processes, including an overreaction of the immune system. Factors that may trigger these ulcers include stress, fatigue, illness, accidental biting, hormonal changes, menstruation, sudden weight loss, food allergies, and deficiencies in vitamin B12, iron, or folic acid. Certain medications, such as nicorandil, and recreational drugs have also been associated with oral ulcers. Additionally, consuming excessive amounts of sour foods can contribute to their development. Trauma Minor physical injuries are a frequent cause of oral ulcers. These injuries may result from sharp edges of teeth, accidental biting (especially involving sharp canine teeth), abrasive or sharp foods, poorly fitting dentures, dental braces, or trauma from toothbrushes. Such ulcers typically heal at a moderate pace if the source of the injury is removed, such as replacing poorly fitting dentures. Chemical Injuries Chemicals like aspirin or alcohol that come into contact with the oral mucosa can cause tissue necrosis, leading to ulceration. Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), a common ingredient in many toothpastes, has been implicated in increasing the incidence of oral ulcers. Infections Viral, bacterial, and fungal infections can all lead to oral ulceration. Viral Infections: The herpes simplex virus is the most common cause of recurrent herpetiform ulcers, which are preceded by painful vesicles that eventually burst. Other viral causes include herpes zoster (shingles), varicella zoster (chickenpox), and Coxsackie A virus. HIV-induced immunodeficiency can also predispose individuals to opportunistic infections and neoplasms, leading to oral ulcers. Bacterial Infections: Bacterial processes such as tuberculosis (caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis) and syphilis (caused by Treponema pallidum) can result in oral ulceration. Additionally, opportunistic activity by normal oral bacteria, such as aerobic streptococci, Neisseria, Actinomyces, spirochetes, and Bacteroides species, can prolong the ulcerative process. Fungal Infections: Fungal pathogens like Coccidioides immitis (valley fever), Cryptococcus neoformans (cryptococcosis), and Blastomyces dermatitidis (North American blastomycosis) can also cause oral ulcers. Immune System-Related Causes Many researchers believe that aphthous ulcers are the result of various disease processes mediated by the immune system. These ulcers may form when the body identifies and attacks unfamiliar chemical molecules, triggering a lymphocyte-mediated response that damages the oral tissues. Immunodeficiency: Recurrent oral ulcers may indicate an underlying immunodeficiency, such as low levels of immunoglobulin in the oral mucosa. Conditions like HIV and chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression are common causes of such deficiencies, making oral ulcers a frequent manifestation. Autoimmunity: Autoimmune conditions, such as mucous membrane pemphigoid, involve an immune reaction against the epithelial basement membrane, leading to desquamation and ulceration of the oral mucosa. Allergy: Contact with allergens can also result in mucosal ulceration. Dietary Factors Deficiencies in vitamin C can lead to scurvy, impairing wound healing and contributing to ulcer formation. Similarly, deficiencies in vitamin B12, iron, zinc, and folic acid have been linked to oral ulcers. Coeliac disease, triggered by the consumption of gluten-containing foods like wheat, rye, and barley, can cause chronic oral ulcers. Avoiding gluten-containing products and substituting them with gluten-free alternatives can help prevent these ulcers. Artificial sweeteners, such as those found in diet sodas and sugarless gum, have also been reported as potential causes of oral ulcers. Cancer Oral cancers can lead to ulceration as the central part of the lesion loses blood supply and undergoes necrosis. Squamous cell carcinoma is one example of such cancers. Symptoms The symptoms preceding an oral ulcer vary depending on the underlying cause. Some ulcers begin with a sharp stinging or burning sensation at the site, which progresses over a few days to form a red spot or bump, eventually developing into an open ulcer. The ulcer typically appears as a white or yellow oval with an inflamed red border. In some cases, a white halo or circle may surround the lesion. The central area of the ulcer often has a gray, white, or yellow appearance due to the presence of fibrin, a protein involved in blood clotting. Oral ulcers are often extremely painful, especially when irritated, and may be accompanied by painful swelling of the lymph nodes beneath the jaw, which can sometimes be mistaken for a toothache. In some cases, other areas of the mouth may become inflamed, with rough-feeling red bumps. Any inflamed area in the mouth that persists for more than two weeks should be evaluated by a doctor or dentist, as it could be a warning sign of oral cancer. Treatment The treatment of oral ulcers typically involves addressing the underlying cause. Correcting imbalances in vitamins and minerals, managing or restricting disease processes, and treating infections can help reduce ulcer formation. For trauma-related ulcers, removing the source of injury (e.g., replacing poorly fitting dentures) can prevent further ulceration. However, since trauma is often accidental, prevention may not always be practical. Individuals prone to opportunistic bacterial infections following oral injuries can prevent infection by rinsing the wound with an antibacterial mouthwash for one minute every 12 hours for two days. It is important to use a small amount of mouthwash (around 1 mL) to avoid adverse effects, such as prolonged taste impairment or disruption of beneficial oral flora. Ideally, the first treatment should occur within three hours of the injury. Subsequent rinses, as directed by the manufacturer, can also be beneficial.
